note: Edge cases where query engines most often disagree. Every probe is deterministic: it orders its own output, aliases every projection, and avoids anything the SQL standard leaves open, unless `known_difference` records the divergence on purpose.

probes.sql: SELECT 3 AS probe WHERE 3 NOT IN (1, 2, NULL)
probes.why: Three-valued logic: `x NOT IN (1, 2, NULL)` can never be TRUE, so the row must be filtered out.

probes.sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS c FROM probe_values WHERE v_int NOT IN (1, 2, NULL)
probes.why: Same three-valued rule applied to a column; any engine returning a count here is wrong.

probes.sql: SELECT SUM(v_int) AS s, COUNT(v_int) AS c, COUNT(*) AS n FROM probe_values WHERE FALSE
probes.why: SUM over an empty set is NULL while COUNT is 0.

probes.sql: SELECT (NULL = NULL) AS r
probes.why: Equality with NULL is unknown, not true.

probes.sql: SELECT (v_text || 'x') AS r FROM probe_values WHERE id = 4
probes.why: `||` propagates NULL.

probes.sql: SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT v_int) AS c FROM probe_values
probes.why: DISTINCT ignores NULLs.

probes.sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS c FROM (SELECT DISTINCT g FROM probe_values) t
probes.why: DISTINCT collapses NULLs to a single group.

probes.sql: SELECT id FROM probe_values ORDER BY g ASC NULLS FIRST, id ASC LIMIT 3
probes.why: Explicit NULLS FIRST placement.

probes.sql: SELECT id FROM probe_values ORDER BY g DESC NULLS LAST, id ASC LIMIT 3
probes.why: Explicit NULLS LAST placement on a DESC key.

probes.sql: SELECT id FROM probe_values ORDER BY g ASC, id ASC LIMIT 3
probes.why: The implicit NULL placement must match the documented default.

probes.sql: SELECT v_int * 2 AS doubled FROM probe_values WHERE v_int IS NOT NULL ORDER BY doubled DESC, v_int ASC
probes.why: ORDER BY on a projection alias.

probes.sql: SELECT g, COUNT(*) AS n FROM probe_values GROUP BY g ORDER BY g NULLS FIRST
probes.why: NULL forms its own group.

probes.sql: SELECT 7 / 2 AS r
probes.known_difference: DuckDB's `/` always yields DOUBLE; DataFusion follows the standard's integer division. Compare manually.
probes.why: Kept in the catalogue as documentation of a deliberate dialect divergence.

probes.sql: SELECT (-7) % 3 AS r
probes.why: Sign of the remainder follows the dividend in the standard.

probes.sql: SELECT 7 % (-3) AS r
SELECT 0.1 + 0.2 AS r
SELECT CAST(2.5 AS INT) AS a, CAST(3.5 AS INT) AS b, CAST(-2.5 AS INT) AS c
probes.known_difference: Known upstream: #11886 'Float to int cast behaviour'. DataFusion truncates toward zero (2.5 -> 2, 1.999 -> 1) while the standard/PostgreSQL/DuckDB round half away from zero.

probes.sql: SELECT CAST('  12  ' AS INT) AS r
SELECT CAST('abc' AS INT) AS r
probes.why: Both engines should reject this; the probe is here to catch a silent 0 or NULL.

probes.sql: SELECT CAST('1e3' AS DOUBLE) AS r
SELECT CAST('2024-02-30' AS DATE) AS r
probes.why: 2024-02-30 does not exist; a silent wrap to 2024-03-01 would be a bug.

probes.sql: SELECT CAST(NULL AS INT) AS r
SELECT ROUND(2.5) AS a, ROUND(-2.5) AS b, ROUND(2.567, 2) AS c, ROUND(1.005, 2) AS d
probes.known_difference: Literal typing: DuckDB parses a bare `1.005` as DECIMAL and rounds exactly, DataFusion as DOUBLE where 1.005 is really 1.00499..., so ROUND gives 1.00. Not an arithmetic bug.

probes.sql: SELECT FLOOR(-2.5) AS f, CEIL(-2.5) AS c, TRUNC(-2.5) AS t

probes.why: Must raise an overflow error rather than wrap around in ANSI mode; in the default non-ANSI mode it is expected to wrap (see `integer_overflow_ansi`).
probes.known_difference: Not a bug: DataFusion defaults to `datafusion.execution.enable_ansi_mode=false`, where integer overflow wraps (Spark-compatible). The ANSI-side expectation is the separate probe `integer_overflow_ansi`, which now runs with `--session-option`; the gap it shows is tracked upstream by the epic #23929.

probes.sql: SELECT AVG(v_int) AS r FROM probe_values
SELECT STDDEV(v_int) AS s, STDDEV_POP(v_int) AS p FROM probe_values WHERE id = 1
SELECT STDDEV(v_int) AS s FROM probe_values WHERE v_int IS NULL
SELECT SUM(v_int) AS s FROM probe_values WHERE v_int IS NULL
SELECT MIN(v_text) AS lo, MAX(v_text) AS hi FROM probe_values WHERE v_text IS NOT NULL
SELECT g, SUM(v_int) AS s, AVG(v_dbl) AS a FROM probe_values GROUP BY g ORDER BY g NULLS FIRST
SELECT id, SUM(v_int) OVER (PARTITION BY g ORDER BY id ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS s FROM probe_values ORDER BY g NULLS FIRST, id
SELECT id, SUM(v_int) OVER (ORDER BY v_int RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS s FROM probe_values WHERE v_int IS NOT NULL ORDER BY v_int, id
probes.why: RANGE includes peer rows with an equal ordering key, ROWS does not. The key is an integer so the probe tests frames, not float ordering.

probes.sql: SELECT id, SUM(v_int) OVER (ORDER BY v_int ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS s FROM probe_values WHERE v_int IS NOT NULL ORDER BY v_int, id
probes.why: RANGE includes peer rows with an equal ordering key, ROWS does not. The key is an integer so the probe tests frames, not float ordering.

probes.sql: SELECT id, LAG(v_int, 1, -1) OVER (PARTITION BY g ORDER BY id) AS prev FROM probe_values ORDER BY g NULLS FIRST, id
SELECT id, NTILE(4) OVER (ORDER BY id) AS bucket FROM probe_values ORDER BY id

SELECT id, FIRST_VALUE(v_int) OVER (PARTITION BY g ORDER BY id ROWS BETWEEN CURRENT ROW AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING) AS f, LAST_VALUE(v_int) OVER (PARTITION BY g ORDER BY id ROWS BETWEEN CURRENT ROW AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING) AS l FROM probe_values ORDER BY g NULLS FIRST, id
SELECT id, SUM(v_int) OVER (PARTITION BY g) AS s FROM probe_values ORDER BY g NULLS FIRST, id
probes.why: A NULL partition key still forms a partition.

probes.sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS c FROM probe_values a LEFT JOIN probe_values b ON a.g = b.g WHERE a.g IS NULL
probes.why: NULL never matches NULL in a join predicate.

probes.sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS c FROM probe_values a FULL OUTER JOIN probe_values b ON a.id = b.g
SELECT COUNT(*) AS c FROM probe_values a WHERE a.g IN (SELECT g FROM probe_values WHERE g IS NOT NULL)
SELECT LENGTH('héllo') AS a, LENGTH('日本語') AS b, LENGTH('') AS c
SELECT SUBSTRING('héllo', 2, 2) AS a, SUBSTRING('日本語', 2, 1) AS b
SELECT UPPER('ß') AS r
probes.why: Uppercasing ß is locale dependent; the result must at least be stable and documented.
probes.known_difference: Unicode full case folding (ß -> SS) in DataFusion versus simple case mapping (ß -> ẞ) in DuckDB. Both defensible; recorded so the daily hunt does not re-report it.

probes.sql: SELECT ('a' LIKE 'A') AS a, ('a' ILIKE 'A') AS b
SELECT TRIM('  x  ') AS a, LTRIM('  x  ') AS b, RTRIM('  x  ') AS c, TRIM(BOTH 'x' FROM 'xxaxx') AS d
SELECT REPLACE('abc', '', 'X') AS r
SELECT CONCAT('a', NULL) AS a, ('a' || NULL) AS b
SELECT GREATEST(NULL, 1) AS g, LEAST(NULL, 1) AS l
probes.why: Postgres ignores NULLs here; the standard leaves it open, so this probe mostly documents behaviour.

probes.sql: SELECT DATE_TRUNC('month', DATE '2024-03-15') AS r
SELECT DATE '2024-02-29' + INTERVAL '1' YEAR AS r
probes.why: Adding a year to a leap day has no obvious answer; behaviour must not be a silent panic.
probes.known_difference: Type divergence, low priority: DATE + INTERVAL yields DATE in DataFusion and TIMESTAMP in DuckDB/PostgreSQL. Surfaced here so it is not re-triaged as new.

probes.sql: SELECT DATE '2024-03-01' - DATE '2024-02-01' AS r
SELECT EXTRACT(DOW FROM DATE '2024-03-17') AS dow, EXTRACT(DOY FROM DATE '2024-03-17') AS doy
SELECT CAST('2024-03-15 12:34:56.789' AS TIMESTAMP) AS r
WITH s AS (SELECT g, COUNT(*) AS n FROM probe_values GROUP BY g) SELECT (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM s) AS groups, (SELECT SUM(n) FROM s) AS rows
probes.why: CTEs plus scalar subqueries must agree on row counts.

probes.sql: SELECT (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM (SELECT g FROM probe_values UNION ALL SELECT g FROM probe_values) t) AS all_rows, (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM (SELECT g FROM probe_values UNION SELECT g FROM probe_values) t) AS distinct_rows
SELECT SUM(CASE WHEN v_int IS NULL THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS nulls, SUM(CASE v_int WHEN 4 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS fours FROM probe_values
SELECT COALESCE(NULL, NULL, 3) AS c, NULLIF(1, 1) AS n, NULLIF(1, 2) AS m
SELECT COUNT(*) AS c FROM probe_values WHERE v_int IN (1 + 1, 4)
SELECT x FROM (VALUES (0.0),(-0.0),(1.0)) AS t(x) ORDER BY x, 1
probes.known_difference: DataFusion sorts with the float total ordering, so -0.0 sorts before 0.0, while `=`, GROUP BY and DISTINCT treat them as equal. That split is deliberate, and the grouped MIN/MAX accumulators were brought in line with it by #24432 (closed as completed 2026-08-20) -- before that fix they used `partial_cmp`, so grouped MIN/MAX were order-dependent and could keep whichever zero came first. DuckDB uses IEEE ordering throughout. Documented, not a bug.
probes.why: Pins the total-ordering decision so a regression would be visible.

probes.sql: SELECT (-0.0 = 0.0) AS equal, COUNT(DISTINCT x) AS distinct_count FROM (VALUES (0.0),(-0.0)) AS t(x)
probes.why: Equality and DISTINCT use IEEE semantics even though ORDER BY uses total ordering.

probes.sql: SELECT map_extract(MAP {'a': 1, 'b': 2}, 'a') AS present, map_extract(MAP {'a': 1}, 'zz') AS missing
probes.why: DataFusion documents `map_extract` as returning a list, empty when the key is absent; DuckDB has the same function, so this is oracle-comparable.

probes.sql: SELECT element_at(MAP {'a': 1}, 'a') AS r
probes.known_difference: In DataFusion `element_at` is documented as an alias of `map_extract` (see information_schema.routines), while DuckDB's `element_at` is array access. Pinned so the divergence is not re-triaged as a bug; note that `element_at(<list>, i)` in DataFusion fails with a user-hostile error, recorded separately.
probes.why: Pins the documented alias so a change in either direction is visible.

probes.sql: SELECT CAST('1.10' AS DECIMAL(10,2)) * CAST('2.00' AS DECIMAL(10,2)) AS m, CAST('2.50' AS DECIMAL(4,2)) + CAST('0.05' AS DECIMAL(4,2)) AS a
probes.why: Decimal multiplication must widen the scale (2 + 2 = 4) rather than fall back to floating point, and decimal addition must stay exact -- 0.05 has no binary representation, so a silent promotion to DOUBLE shows up here.

probes.sql: SELECT CAST('1.00' AS DECIMAL(4,2)) / CAST('3.00' AS DECIMAL(4,2)) AS d
probes.why: Decimal division has no standardised result scale; the point of the probe is that DataFusion keeps a decimal result here and neither loses the type nor crashes.
probes.known_difference: Dialect divergence, not a bug: DataFusion keeps DECIMAL and applies its own result scale (scale 6 here -> 0.333333), while DuckDB promotes the result to DOUBLE (0.3333333333333333). DataFusion's decimal division rules are its own compatibility choice, tracked upstream as #7301 'Decimal division compatibility mode with spark'. Recorded so it is not re-triaged as a bug.

probes.sql: SELECT COALESCE(g, -1) AS g_key, COUNT(*) AS c FROM probe_values GROUP BY GROUPING SETS ((g), ()) ORDER BY g_key, c
probes.why: GROUPING SETS must emit one row per grouping set, including the grand total over all 12 rows, and the NULL group must not be merged into it.

probes.sql: SELECT 0.1 + 0.2 AS r
probes.why: The first probe that exercises --session-option: with float literals parsed as DECIMAL the sum is exactly 0.3, which is also what DuckDB's DECIMAL literals give. It fails loudly if the option is ever silently ignored, which is the failure mode a session-option flag has.

Same expression as `integer_overflow`, with ANSI mode on: `enable_ansi_mode`'s own documentation promises that 'numeric overflow ... raise[s] runtime errors rather than returning NULL or adjusted values', so all three columns should be errors.
probes.known_difference: Known upstream: the ANSI mode epic #23929 names arithmetic overflow as in scope ('for example, invalid casts, arithmetic overflow, division by zero') and #24950 covers the spark-specific cast-overflow case. Measured 2026-10-15 on 55.2.0 with `enable_ansi_mode=true`: the three expressions still wrap to -9223372036854775808 / 9223372036854775807 / -2, i.e. the config documentation is ahead of the implementation. Recorded here so no slot re-files it as a new bug; revisit when #23929 lands.

probes.sql: SELECT COALESCE(g, -1) AS g_key, grouping(g) AS is_total, COUNT(*) AS c FROM probe_values GROUP BY ROLLUP(g) ORDER BY g_key, c
probes.why: ROLLUP must emit the same groups as the equivalent GROUPING SETS list, and `grouping(g)` must separate the NULL-valued group (`is_total = 0`, 2 rows) from the grand total (`is_total = 1`, all 12) -- the whole point of the flag, and the thing a plain COALESCE cannot tell apart.

probes.sql: SELECT id, SUM(v_int) OVER (ORDER BY v_int RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS s FROM probe_values ORDER BY id
probes.why: A RANGE frame is peer-based, not row-based: every row whose ORDER BY value ties must see the same running sum, and the NULL ordering value forms one peer group at the end. `probe_values` has ties (4,4 and 5,5) and NULLs precisely for this, and row-based `ROWS` semantics would give different numbers.

probes.sql: SELECT 'intersect_all' AS op, v FROM (SELECT v FROM (VALUES (1),(1),(1),(2)) t(v) INTERSECT ALL SELECT v FROM (VALUES (1),(1),(3)) u(v)) x UNION ALL SELECT 'except_all' AS op, v FROM (SELECT v FROM (VALUES (1),(1),(1),(2)) t(v) EXCEPT ALL SELECT v FROM (VALUES (1),(1),(3)) u(v)) y ORDER BY op, v
probes.why: The ALL variants of INTERSECT/EXCEPT are multiset operators with standard-fixed answers: with T1={1,1,1,2} (m copies) and T2={1,1,3} (n copies), INTERSECT ALL must emit min(m,n) copies of each row -- 1,1 -- and EXCEPT ALL must emit max(m-n,0) -- 1,2. One probe covers both operators because the same input pair drives both, and the `op` column keeps the two answers distinguishable.
probes.known_difference: Known upstream, already open -- not a new bug. DataFusion's ALL set operators do not implement multiset semantics. Measured 2026-10-15 on 55.2.0 (1 and 4 partitions identical, so it is not a planning artifact): INTERSECT ALL returns 1,1,1 (all three LHS copies) where the standard and DuckDB give 1,1; EXCEPT ALL returns only 2 where the standard and DuckDB give 1,2, i.e. it removes every LHS copy of a row that appears at all on the RHS. Filed upstream as apache/datafusion#12955 'INTERSECT ALL returns wrong number of records from RHS' and #12956 'EXCEPT ALL returns the wrong number of records' (both open since 2024-10-15, both quoting the same SQL-92 paragraph). Recorded here so no slot re-files it as new; revisit when either issue is fixed, and flip this probe to a pinned `expect_rows` at that point.

probes.sql: SELECT 'gs' AS src, value AS v FROM generate_series(1,5) AS g(value) UNION ALL SELECT 'range' AS src, value AS v FROM range(5,-1,-2) AS r(value) ORDER BY src, v
probes.why: First coverage of the TABLE function family: `information_schema.routines` lists exactly two functions with function_type='TABLE' (`generate_series`, `range`) and nothing -- neither a probe nor `df_robust.py --function-type` -- had ever exercised them. Covers both functions, ascending and descending steps in one query. `range` is end-exclusive, so `range(5,-1,-2)` must stop before -1 and yield 5,3,1 (a difference in end-exclusivity or step direction is visible in the pinned rows).

probes.sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS c, MIN(v) AS lo, MAX(v) AS hi FROM generate_series(1, 9223372036854775806, 9223372036854775805) AS g(v)
probes.why: The series generator has to advance with a checked add: the naive `current + step` overflows i64 here (1 + i64::MAX-ish), and an overflow in a `next` computation is a PANIC-class regression, not a wrong answer. The correct series is [1, 9223372036854775806], i.e. exactly two rows, so the probe is bounded and safe to run every slot. Verified 2026-10-16 on 55.2.0: no panic, no wrap.

probes.sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS c, MIN(CAST(v AS DATE)) AS lo, MAX(CAST(v AS DATE)) AS hi FROM generate_series(DATE '2024-01-01', DATE '2024-01-03', INTERVAL '1' DAY) AS g(v)
probes.why: The third argument of `generate_series` is an interval when the bounds are DATE/TIMESTAMP, a different code path from the integer form; the endpoints are asserted as DATEs so the pinned answer is free of timestamp-rendering differences between the engines. Three days inclusive must give three rows.

probes.sql: SELECT i, nth_value(x, 0) OVER (ORDER BY i) AS n FROM (VALUES (1, 1), (2, 2), (3, 3)) t(i, x) ORDER BY i
probes.why: Pins the window form's answer for a zero index, which is NULL for every row in *both* engines. It matters because the aggregate form of the same call is a different story: `nth_value(x, 0)` without OVER rejects 0, and until 2026-10-17 it rejected it with an internal error asking the user to file a bug report. That asymmetry is deliberate on the window side -- upstream asserts it in window.slt under the heading 'test handle NULL and 0 value of nth_value' (NULL, an expression evaluating to NULL, and 0 all give NULL) -- so this probe records the intended behaviour rather than inviting a later slot to 'fix' it. Changing it would be a behaviour change, not a bug fix.
probes.known_difference: Not a divergence: DuckDB also returns NULL for a zero index in the window form, so the probe compares equal. Recorded in `why` for the aggregate/window asymmetry only.

probes.sql: SELECT split_part('a,b,c', ',', 1) AS a, split_part('a,b,c', ',', 2) AS b, split_part('a,b,c', ',', -1) AS c, split_part('a,b,c', ',', 4) AS d
probes.why: The field index is 1-based, negative counts back from the end (-1 -> 'c'), and an index past the last field yields the empty string (4 -> ''). Nothing in the catalogue covered string splitting, and index handling is where string functions usually go wrong. Both engines agree on all four columns. Index 0 is deliberately not in this probe: DataFusion rejects it with 'Execution error: field position must not be zero' while DuckDB returns '', a dialect difference that would only produce a false candidate.

probes.sql: SELECT date_part('week', DATE '2024-01-01') AS w1, date_part('week', DATE '2023-01-01') AS w2
probes.why: ISO-8601 week numbering has a trap: 2024-01-01 is week 1, but 2023-01-01 belongs to week 52 of 2022 (2023 started on a Sunday, so its first ISO week begins on 2023-01-02). An implementation that does US-style week numbering, or that simply divides the day-of-year by 7, returns 1 for the second column. Both engines return the ISO answer; the pinned rows make a regression visible without an oracle.

probes.sql: SELECT * EXCLUDE (v_text) FROM probe_values ORDER BY id LIMIT 3
probes.why: `SELECT * EXCLUDE (col)` is a recent SQL surface that nothing in the catalogue covered. The dropped column must be gone and the remaining columns must stay in table order; a projection bug here would swap or repeat columns, which the pinned rows show up immediately. DuckDB agrees.

probes.sql: SELECT COALESCE(g, -1) AS g_key, COUNT(*) AS c FROM probe_values GROUP BY ALL ORDER BY g_key
probes.why: `GROUP BY ALL` must group by every non-aggregated projection expression -- here the COALESCE, not the bare `g` -- and the NULL group has to survive as its own group (2 rows in probe_values), because NULL is a group key like any other. Pinning both facts at once. Caution for future slots: write the plain `SELECT g, COUNT(*) ... GROUP BY ALL` form instead and the probe diverges, because DuckDB drops the NULL group there; keep the COALESCE so the two engines stay comparable.

probes.sql: SELECT x, COUNT(*) OVER (PARTITION BY x) AS n FROM (VALUES (0.0), (-0.0), (1.0)) t(x) ORDER BY n, x
probes.why: Signed zero is the sharpest test of what an engine means by "equal enough to group together": 0.0 = -0.0 is true, so a PARTITION BY that treats them as equal gives n = 2 for both rows, and one that compares bit patterns gives n = 1 for each. The probe is here because DataFusion answers the two ways in the same engine: `GROUP BY x` merges them (n = 2), the window path does not (n = 1) -- and DuckDB merges them in both.
probes.known_difference: Known upstream, still open -- do not re-file. apache/datafusion#25766 'Window PARTITION BY puts 0.0 and -0.0 in separate partitions' (open since 2026-09-26). Measured 2026-10-17 on the pinned 55.2.0 *and* on main via the sqllogictest runner: the window path returns n = 1 for 0.0, -0.0 and 1.0 (three partitions), while `GROUP BY x` on the same values returns n = 2 for the two zeros. DuckDB groups them in both cases. The asymmetry with DataFusion's own GROUP BY is the strongest evidence that the window path is the wrong side of the inconsistency; recorded here so no slot re-triages it, and so a fix upstream is visible.

probes.sql: SELECT NULL IS DISTINCT FROM NULL AS a, 1 IS DISTINCT FROM NULL AS b, NULL IS NOT DISTINCT FROM NULL AS c, 1 IS DISTINCT FROM 1 AS d
probes.why: `IS DISTINCT FROM` is the null-safe comparison the catalogue had no coverage for, and it is the one comparison operator whose answer never depends on three-valued logic: NULL IS DISTINCT FROM NULL is false (they are not distinct), 1 IS DISTINCT FROM NULL is true, and the NOT form inverts that. Worth pinning separately from the = / <> probes precisely because implementations often reuse the three-valued code path and get the NULL/NULL case wrong.

probes.sql: SELECT date_bin(INTERVAL '15 minutes', TIMESTAMP '2024-01-01 12:37:45') AS floor_in_bin, date_bin(INTERVAL '15 minutes', TIMESTAMP '2024-01-01 12:30:00') AS on_boundary, date_bin(INTERVAL '1 hour', TIMESTAMP '2024-01-01 12:37:45', TIMESTAMP '2024-01-01 00:30:00') AS origin_0030, date_bin(INTERVAL '1 hour', TIMESTAMP '2024-01-01 12:29:59', TIMESTAMP '2024-01-01 00:30:00') AS origin_0030_before, date_bin(INTERVAL '7 days', TIMESTAMP '2024-01-05 00:00:00') AS week_from_epoch
probes.why: The five columns pin the whole bucketing rule at once, which is where `date_bin` bugs live: a value inside a bin floors to its start; a value sitting exactly on a boundary stays there (no off-by-one); an explicit origin shifts the grid (bins at :30, so 12:29:59 falls back to 11:30, not 12:30); and without an origin the bins are anchored to the 1970-01-01 epoch rather than to the row or to year boundaries -- 2024-01-05 in 7-day bins starts at 2024-01-04, which is 2818 whole weeks after the epoch. A change in any of those four behaviours shows up as a failed expectation.
probes.known_difference: DuckDB has no `date_bin` (it spells the operation `time_bucket`, which is also anchored differently in its origin handling), so the oracle cannot check this one; the pinned rows are the specification. Recorded so the ERROR_DIVERGENCE from DuckDB's missing function is not re-triaged as a DataFusion bug.

probes.sql: SELECT v, PERCENT_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY v) AS pr, CUME_DIST() OVER (ORDER BY v) AS cd FROM (VALUES (1), (2), (2), (4)) t(v) ORDER BY v
probes.why: Both formulas are fixed by the standard and both are easy to get subtly wrong once there are ties: PERCENT_RANK is (rank - 1) / (rows - 1) -- rank, not row number, so the two rows with v = 2 share 1/3 and the answer must not be (row_number - 1) / 3 -- and CUME_DIST is (rows <= current) / rows, so the tied pair shares 3/4 instead of 2/4. The pair also pins that correct ranks are not compressed (v = 4 is 1.0, not 0.66).

probes.sql: SELECT v, SUM(v) OVER (ORDER BY v GROUPS BETWEEN 1 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS s FROM (VALUES (1), (2), (2), (4)) t(v) ORDER BY v
probes.why: GROUPS is the third frame mode and the only one the catalogue did not cover: it counts *peer groups*, not rows (ROWS) or values (RANGE). With peers {1}, {2, 2}, {4}, one preceding group makes the second group sum 1 + 2 + 2 = 5 (12 with a ROWS frame would give 1 + 2 = 3) and the last 2 + 2 + 4 = 8 (4 + 4 = 8 with ROWS). A frame implementation that treats GROUPS as ROWS fails on the middle and last rows.

probes.sql: SELECT v, SUM(v) FILTER (WHERE v > 1) OVER (ORDER BY v ROWS UNBOUNDED PRECEDING) AS s FROM (VALUES (1), (2), (3)) t(v) ORDER BY v
probes.why: A FILTER clause attached to an aggregate that is *also* a window function: the filter removes rows from the frame before aggregating, so the first row's frame is empty and SUM over an empty set is NULL (three-valued logic, not 0), then 2 and 5. Pinning this catches both a filter that is ignored and one that wrongly yields 0 for the empty frame.

probes.sql: SELECT EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM TIMESTAMP '2024-01-01 00:00:00') AS ts_epoch, EXTRACT(EPOCH FROM DATE '2024-01-01') AS date_epoch
probes.why: Epoch extraction is where unit and timezone mistakes hide: the answer must be seconds since 1970-01-01T00:00:00Z, identical for a DATE and for the TIMESTAMP at its midnight, and it must not be shifted by the session timezone. 1704067200 is the value for 2024-01-01; a millisecond implementation, a local-time implementation or an off-by-one on the DATE path all miss it.

probes.sql: SELECT SUBSTRING('abcdef' FROM 2 FOR 3) AS with_for, SUBSTRING('abcdef' FROM 4) AS from_only
probes.why: The SQL-standard `SUBSTRING(x FROM n [FOR m])` spelling is a different parser path from the `substring(x, n, m)` function call, and the FOR-less form has to run to the end of the string. Both give the 1-based answer here, so a regression that ignores FOR or that truncates the FOR-less form is visible without an oracle.

probes.sql: SELECT COALESCE(g, -1) AS g_key, COUNT(*) FILTER (WHERE v_int > 0) AS c FROM probe_values GROUP BY GROUPING SETS ((g), ()) ORDER BY g_key, c
probes.why: A FILTER inside a GROUPING SETS aggregate: the filter has to apply per row before the set is aggregated, and the grand total has to count only the filtered rows across the whole table (8 of 12), not per group. The -1 rows are the grand total of both sets, ordered after the real groups so the pinned order is unambiguous.

probes.sql: SELECT CAST(DATE '2024-01-31' + INTERVAL '1' MONTH AS DATE) AS jan31_plus1, CAST(DATE '2024-01-30' + INTERVAL '1' MONTH AS DATE) AS jan30_plus1, CAST(DATE '2024-03-31' - INTERVAL '1' MONTH AS DATE) AS mar31_minus1
probes.why: Month arithmetic on a day the target month does not have must clamp to that month's last day: 31 January + 1 month is 29 February 2024, not 2 March and not an error, and 31 March - 1 month is also 29 February. 2024 is a leap year, so a non-leap implementation or an overflow-to-next-month implementation both show up here. The CAST pins the result as DATE so the DATE-versus-TIMESTAMP divergence recorded in `date_add_year_leap` cannot hide the rule.

probes.sql: SELECT POSITION('b' IN 'abc') AS found, POSITION('' IN 'abc') AS empty_needle, POSITION('z' IN 'abc') AS absent
probes.why: The SQL-standard `POSITION(x IN y)` spelling is a distinct parser path from the `strpos` function, and POSITION is 1-based with 0 meaning absent -- not -1, which is what a strpos-shaped implementation would return. An empty needle matches at position 1.

probes.sql: SELECT x, SUM(x) OVER (ORDER BY x RANGE BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS s FROM (VALUES (1),(2),(2),(3)) AS t(x) ORDER BY x, s
probes.why: An offset boundary in RANGE mode is value-based and includes peers: the frame for x=2 is every row whose key lies in [0,2], so both 2s get 1+2+2=5, and x=3 reaches back to 1 for 8. A ROWS-shaped implementation of the same clause would give 1,2,4,6, so the offset semantics are pinned without an oracle.

probes.sql: SELECT string_agg(v, ',' ORDER BY v DESC) AS s FROM (VALUES ('a'),('c'),('b')) AS t(v)
probes.why: The aggregate-level ORDER BY clause (inside the call, not the query's ORDER BY) decides the order the aggregate sees: descending here, so the separator-joined string must be c,b,a. An implementation that ignores the inner ORDER BY, or that applies it after aggregation, produces a,b,c. Pinned as a scalar string so the comparison is exact.

probes.sql: SELECT x, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY x) AS rn FROM (VALUES (2),(NULL),(1)) AS t(x) ORDER BY rn
probes.why: The default null placement of a window's ORDER BY (NULLS LAST for ASC here) is a separate code path from a query-level ORDER BY, and it decides the row numbers: the NULL must get rn=3, not rn=1. Pinned by ordering the output on rn, so the null's position is asserted rather than left to the renderer.

probes.sql: SELECT g, COUNT(*) AS n FROM (VALUES (1,10),(1,20),(2,5)) AS t(g,v) GROUP BY g HAVING SUM(v) > 10 ORDER BY g
probes.why: HAVING may filter on an aggregate that the projection does not select (SUM(v) here, while the output is g and COUNT(*)). The group with SUM(v)=5 must be dropped and the other kept with n=2; an implementation that rewrites HAVING into a projection-level filter or that recomputes the aggregate differently shows up as either two rows or a wrong count.

probes.sql: SELECT CAST(DATE_TRUNC('week', DATE '2024-01-03') AS DATE) AS mid_week, CAST(DATE_TRUNC('week', DATE '2024-01-01') AS DATE) AS monday
probes.why: Week truncation is anchored on Monday: Wednesday 2024-01-03 truncates back to Monday 2024-01-01, and a Monday truncates to itself. A Sunday-anchored implementation gives 2023-12-31 for the first value, and a timestamp-returning one hides the anchor behind a time-of-day. Cast to DATE so the answer is compared as a date.

probes.sql: SELECT lpad('abc', 2, 'x') AS truncated, rpad('abc', 5, 'xy') AS padded, lpad('7', 3, '0') AS zeros
probes.why: Three rules in one call: a target length shorter than the value truncates it (abc -> ab, from the right), a longer one pads cyclically with the fill string (abc + xy -> abcxy, not abcxyxy cut arbitrarily), and lpad pads on the left (7 -> 007). Catches pad-on-the-wrong-side, non-cyclic padding and truncate-to-empty.

probes.sql: SELECT SUM(CASE WHEN x = 1 THEN 1 END) AS s, COUNT(*) AS n, COUNT(CASE WHEN x = 1 THEN 1 END) AS c FROM (VALUES (1),(2),(3)) AS t(x)
probes.why: A CASE with no ELSE yields NULL for the rows it does not match, and the aggregates must treat that as unknown rather than as zero: SUM skips the NULLs (1, not 3), COUNT(*) still counts every row (3), and COUNT(expr) counts only the non-NULL one (1). An ELSE 0 rewrite keeps SUM right but turns c into 3.

probes.sql: SELECT COUNT(*) AS n, MIN(g) AS surviving FROM (VALUES (1),(2)) AS t(g) GROUP BY g HAVING g > 1
probes.why: HAVING may filter on a grouping column that the projection does not select: only the g=2 group survives, so n=1 and MIN(g)=2 (which is what makes the surviving group identifiable). An implementation that only allows aggregates in HAVING, or that pushes the condition into the projection instead of the group filter, gives either an error or both groups.

probes.sql: SELECT CAST(DATE_TRUNC('quarter', DATE '2024-05-15') AS DATE) AS mid_quarter, CAST(DATE_TRUNC('quarter', DATE '2024-01-01') AS DATE) AS quarter_start
probes.why: Quarter truncation is calendar-anchored, not a rolling 3-month window: 15 May 2024 truncates to 1 April 2024, and a 1 January is already a quarter start. A 90-day rolling implementation or a January-anchored month index both miss the first value; cast to DATE so the anchor is compared as a date.

probes.sql: SELECT length('héllo') AS chars, bit_length('héllo') AS bits
probes.why: Two different counts of the same string: `length` counts characters (5, because é is one character) while `bit_length` counts UTF-8 bytes times eight (é is two bytes, so 6 bytes = 48 bits). An implementation that counts bytes in `length`, or characters in `bit_length`, or that mixes bytes with bits, is visible in one of the two numbers.

probes.sql: SELECT l[1] AS the_first, l[3] AS the_last, l[0] AS index_zero, l[4] AS past_the_end FROM (SELECT [10, 20, 30] AS l) t
probes.why: List indexing is 1-based, and both index 0 and an index past the end must yield NULL rather than an error. A 0-based engine returns 20 and a value here, so the pair pins the base and the out-of-range rule at once.

probes.sql: SELECT (SELECT count(*) FROM (SELECT v FROM (VALUES (1),(1),(NULL)) t(v) INTERSECT SELECT v FROM (VALUES (1),(2),(NULL)) u(v)) x) AS intersect_rows, (SELECT count(*) FROM (SELECT v FROM (VALUES (NULL),(NULL)) t(v) UNION SELECT v FROM (VALUES (NULL)) u(v)) y) AS union_rows
probes.why: Set operations compare with 'not distinct from', so NULL matches NULL even though `NULL = NULL` is unknown, and they deduplicate: the repeated 1 and the repeated NULLs each collapse to one row. Two counts catch an engine that either drops NULL pairs or keeps duplicates.

probes.sql: SELECT a, b, count(*) AS n FROM (VALUES ('x',1),('x',2),('y',1)) t(a,b) GROUP BY CUBE(a,b) ORDER BY a NULLS LAST, b NULLS LAST
probes.why: CUBE(a, b) is the four grouping sets (a, b), (a), (b) and (), each with its own count, so a 3-row input yields 8 rows. The subtotal rows carry NULL in the collapsed column and must not be dropped or merged with a real NULL group.

probes.sql: SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT x) AS distinct_vals, COUNT(*) AS rows_all, SUM(CASE WHEN x = x THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS self_equal_rows FROM (VALUES (CAST('NaN' AS DOUBLE)), (CAST('NaN' AS DOUBLE)), (1.0)) t(x)
probes.why: NaN is one value for DISTINCT and GROUP BY, not one group per row, and `NaN = NaN` is TRUE -- deliberately unlike IEEE 754, which makes every comparison with NaN false. An engine that kept the two NaNs apart would report distinct_vals=3; one that followed IEEE would report self_equal_rows=1.

probes.sql: SELECT isnan(MIN(x)) AS min_is_nan, isnan(MAX(x)) AS max_is_nan, COUNT(x) AS counted, (CAST('NaN' AS DOUBLE) > 1.0) AS nan_above_one FROM (VALUES (CAST('NaN' AS DOUBLE)), (1.0)) t(x)
probes.why: NaN is a value rather than a missing one (COUNT counts it), and under the float total ordering it is larger than every number, so MIN returns the number while MAX returns NaN. Pins the grouped MIN/MAX placement that #24432 had to correct.

probes.sql: SELECT (CAST('-NaN' AS DOUBLE) = CAST('NaN' AS DOUBLE)) AS neg_equals_pos, (CAST('-NaN' AS DOUBLE) > 1.0) AS neg_above_one, (CAST('-NaN' AS DOUBLE) < 1.0) AS neg_below_one
probes.known_difference: DataFusion keeps the sign of NaN: `-NaN = NaN` is false, and the total ordering puts -NaN below every number while NaN sits above them. DuckDB treats every NaN as one value (`true, true, false`). Upstream is moving toward the DuckDB reading -- apache/datafusion#26091 'Treat all NaNs as the same value (`-NaN = NaN`)', with the sign handling tracked in one place by apache/datafusion#26138. Pinned so the change is visible here when it lands.
probes.why: Pins the sign-sensitivity of NaN so that the day #26091 lands, this probe reports a changed answer instead of silently going stale.
